assumptions: USD million and thousand parts. Fictional Finch Components. Compare relevant annual costs; parts required 100k, defect rate applies to purchased units and replacement paid by manufacturer. No taxes or discount.

evidence.text: [Make] Internal variable cost $38 per good part; annual avoidable setup cost .6m. Production capacity used by this component can alternatively generate .9m contribution from product Z only if entire component outsourced.

[Buy] Supplier price $42 per delivered part; expected defect fraction 4% of 100k purchased. For each defective part, supplier replaces free, manufacturer incurs $15 handling. Expected defect handling independent of spare capacity.
[Quality] Internal cost includes defect handling; both options deliver 100k good parts under stated assumptions. Common factory overhead 1.2m allocated to component remains regardless choice.
[Offer] Supplier also offers $40/unit if annual order rises to 120k. Excess 20k not required, no resale or next-year use; all purchase price paid. Defect handling on entire order.
[Transition] One-year decision, switching training cost .15m incurred only if outsource. Alternative Z contribution .9m net of its own incremental costs.
[Memo] Controller treats allocated 1.2m as avoidable and ignores opportunity cost of keeping internal capacity.

qas.question: What is the annual incremental cash cost of internal manufacture before opportunity cost?
What expected defect-handling cost applies to the standard purchase contract?
Calculate relevant cost of outsourcing 100k including transition and foregone/earned alternatives; express cost net of product Z contribution.
Find advantage of standard outsourcing over continuing internal production.
Compute net relevant cost of the 120k discount purchase option.
Why should the common 1.2m overhead not be counted as an outsourcing saving?
qas.answer: It remains regardless of option and therefore cancels in an incremental decision.

qas.question: Should management select the lower $40 quote rather than $42?
qas.answer: No. Excess 20k has no economic use; the total net cost 4.122 exceeds 3.51 for required volume.

qas.question: Can long-term outsourcing risk be ranked with the one-year expected defect data?
qas.answer: No. Future prices, supplier continuity and quality distribution are absent.

assumptions: USD million; thousand units. Fictional Linden Home. Toy promotion changes quantity and price of item X and cannibalizes complementary sales Y as stated; compare incremental contribution. No tax, inventory constraints or common fixed changes.

evidence.text: [Baseline] X sells 80k units at $100, variable cost $60. Y sells 40k at $80, variable cost $50.
[Promotion] X price reduced to $90 for all X units; expected X volume rises to 120k. Y volume falls by 10k due to substitution; Y price/cost unchanged.
[Advertising] Campaign fixed incremental spend .5m. No other fixed costs change. No refunds or timing effects.
[Sensitivity] If campaign results in only 100k X units, Y still falls by 10k and spend .5m unchanged.
[Policy] Compare total contribution from both items after incremental advertising, not gross revenue growth.
[Memo] Marketer reports extra 40k X sales at $30 margin, ignores discount on original 80k and Y loss.

qas.question: Find combined baseline contribution from X and Y.
Determine promoted X contribution before advertising.
Find total promotional result after lost Y sales and campaign cost.
What is incremental contribution versus baseline?
How many thousand X units must sell at $90 to break even on total contribution, holding Y loss fixed?
Why does the proposed extra-unit contribution calculation overstate the benefit?
qas.answer: It omits the $10 price cut on baseline units (0.8m), the 0.3m lost Y contribution and 0.5m campaign cost.

qas.question: Can the 100k downside scenario be interpreted as actual forecast probability?
qas.answer: No. It is a sensitivity outcome with no probability assigned.

qas.question: Can customer lifetime value justify the loss?
qas.answer: Not on supplied evidence. Repeat purchase, retention, acquisition and later margin data are missing.

assumptions: USD million. Fictional Wren Harbor bank. Toy first-order economic value sensitivity to +100bps parallel rates, asset/liability dollar duration given through balances and modified durations. Hedge receives floating/pays fixed; stipulated sensitivity gain per notional.

evidence.text: [Balance] Rate-sensitive assets 1,000m duration 4; liabilities 850m duration 2.5. Economic value change = −asset×duration×shock + liability×duration×shock.
[Hedge quote] Each 100m swap notional yields +3m economic value under +100bps and costs .6m annual carry. Choose 0, 200m, 400m or 600m notional. No counterparty impact.
[Risk rule] Worst allowed economic value decline under specified +100bps shock is 8m. Among qualifying hedges minimize annual carry. Carry budget 3m.
[Other scenario] −100bps parallel rate move gives symmetric first-order value effect; carry unchanged. No convexity in toy.
[Treasury] Current annual NII 45m before hedge carry; toy carry expense reduces NII directly. No other P&L effect in annual base.
[Memo] CFO proposes largest notional to minimize stress loss without checking carry budget.

qas.question: Find unhedged economic value change under +100bps.
Find stress value change with 200m swap notional.
Find value change with 400m notional under the upward shock.
Find annual carry of the 400m hedge.
Determine base annual NII after selecting the minimum-cost feasible hedge.
Why not choose 600m solely because it reduces the upward shock loss further?
qas.answer: Its annual carry is 3.6m, above the 3m budget. 400m already satisfies the specified risk constraint at lower cost.

qas.question: Does this hedge necessarily improve economic value under falling rates?
qas.answer: No. Under symmetric downward move, unhedged gain 18.75 is reduced by swap loss 12; 400m hedge gain is 6.75.

qas.question: Can actual interest rate risk be established for a steepening curve?
qas.answer: No. Key-rate durations, convexity, deposit behavior and nonparallel sensitivities are missing.

assumptions: USD million; thousand policies. Fictional Pine Lantern insurer. Toy 20k identical policies, three exclusive loss outcomes per policy, compare two deductible choices with given premium and retention response. No correlation/tax.

evidence.text: [Loss model per policy] Probability no claim .90; claim $2,000 .08; claim $15,000 .02. Deductible applied per claim, no cap. Claims expected independently for calculation.
[Option L] Deductible $500, annual premium $550, retains all 20k policies. Fixed overhead 2m, servicing $100/policy.
[Option H] Deductible $2,000, annual premium $430, retains 85% of policies, same loss probabilities among retained. Same overhead, servicing $100/policy.
[Policy] Expected annual underwriting result = premium−expected claim payment−servicing−fixed overhead. No investment return.
[Stress] Large-loss probability increases to .03, no-claim declines .01; small claim probability unchanged. Retention unchanged.
[Memo] Actuary compares deductibles only and ignores premium and policy retention.

qas.question: Find expected annual claim payout per policy under low deductible L.
Find expected annual payout per retained policy under H.
Find base underwriting result for L.
Find base underwriting result for H including retention.
Find H underwriting result in large-loss stress.
Which option has higher expected base result, and does either break even?
qas.answer: H has less negative result (−.81 vs −1.2); neither reaches break-even under the supplied model.

qas.question: Why is higher deductible not proof of higher total profit?
qas.answer: It changes expected payouts, but premium and retained policy count also change; fixed overhead remains.

qas.question: Can actual adverse selection after raising deductible be quantified?
qas.answer: No. Same loss probabilities were stipulated; no behavioral data by risk group are given.

assumptions: USD million. Fictional Fern Circuit. Toy three-year make/buy comparison at 10%, all recurring payments year-end. Discount factors .9090909091, .8264462810, .7513148009; no tax or terminal value except stated exit cost.

evidence.text: [Build] Upfront engineering 5m at t0. Annual operating cash expense 1.5m in years1–3. End year3 salvage code license cash .8m; no other value.
[Buy] Upfront integration 1m at t0. Annual vendor fee 2.5m years1–3, support .4m annually. Mandatory exit migration 1.2m at end year3.
[Service] Same performance and revenue; common internal staff cost 2m annually unavoidable and excluded from incremental comparison.
[Liquidity] Maximum upfront spend 4m. Buy can be financed through normal year-end revenue, build upfront cannot be staged or borrowed in toy.
[Valuation] Compare positive PV cost, lower is preferable subject to liquidity. Factors as specified. No uncertainty probabilities.
[Memo] CTO compares only build upfront 5 with annual license 2.5, excludes exit cost and salvage.

qas.question: Find PV of three recurring build costs.
Find total PV cost of build after terminal salvage.
Find total PV cost of buy including support and exit migration.
Find economic PV cost advantage of build ignoring liquidity.
How much does build exceed the upfront budget?
Which option is feasible under the explicit funding restriction?
qas.answer: Buy. Build has lower PV cost but violates the 4m t0 limit; financing or staging is unavailable.

qas.question: Should unavoidable common staff cost be included for deciding incremental preference?
qas.answer: It may appear in full budgets, but it is identical and cancels from incremental comparison.

qas.question: Can security and reliability superiority of either option be inferred from discounted costs?
qas.answer: No. Performance is stipulated equal; no security incident or reliability data are given.

assumptions: USD million; million MWh. Fictional kiln operator. Toy output equal under fuels, emissions and consumption rates supplied. Compare annual incremental cash cost including carbon charge, no tax.

evidence.text: [Output] Annual useful heat 2m MWh, same for both fuel options. Current coal heat cost $25 per useful MWh, emissions .9 tCO2/MWh.
[Gas alternative] Useful heat cost $35/MWh, emissions .35 tCO2/MWh. Requires annual incremental maintenance 3m; conversion upfront 20m, not in annual operating comparison.
[Carbon charge] Current $30/t on all emissions, no free allowances. Sensitivity $60/t. No other pricing or offsets.
[Policy] Annual cost = useful heat cost+carbon charge+incremental maintenance. Simple payback on positive annual savings if unchanged.
[Grant] Approved conversion grant 5m received upfront; net conversion cost 15m. No other capex or subsidies.
[Memo] Manager claims gas must be cheaper because emissions lower; ignores fuel price and maintenance.

qas.question: Find annual emissions avoided by switching from coal to gas.
Find annual coal operating cash cost at current carbon price.
Find annual gas cash cost including additional maintenance.
Find break-even carbon charge for equal annual costs.
Find simple payback after approved grant at current carbon price.
Why is gas not always cheaper just because its emissions are lower?
qas.answer: Fuel and maintenance increase annual cash costs; the carbon savings must cover the difference. Below break-even charge coal is cheaper in this toy.

qas.question: Is the 5m grant an annual reduction of gas fuel cost?
qas.answer: No. It reduces the initial conversion outlay once, not recurring operating cost.

qas.question: Can actual lifetime NPV be established from simple payback?
qas.answer: No. Future carbon/fuel prices, asset life, downtime and discount rate are absent.

assumptions: USD million. Fictional office property. Toy three-year rent choice, discount factors .95, .90, .85 stipulated; no taxes, identical fixed costs. Compare cash incremental contribution only.

evidence.text: [Renewal] Existing tenant accepts 3-year lease at 4m rent annually, tenant incentive 1.2m cash immediately, landlord incremental maintenance .4m/year. No vacancy.

[Replacement] Existing tenant leaves now. New tenant signs contingent lease with first-year rent 1m after vacancy, year2 and year3 rent 5m each; landlord fit-out 2m at t0, leasing fee .5m t0, incremental maintenance .5m annually.
[Cash constraints] Maximum upfront leasing outlay 2m. No borrowing or deferred fit-out allowed.
[Valuation] Use stated year-end discount factors. Fixed property overhead .8m/year unavoidable and excluded; no residual effect.
[Risk] Replacement signed only if owner accepts offer; assume certainty conditional acceptance for toy. No later rent escalations.
[Memo] Broker ranks replacement based only on higher stabilized rent 5m.

qas.question: Find renewal PV of operating cash contribution net of incentive.
Find replacement PV including vacancy period and fit-out/fee.
Find renewal's PV advantage over replacement.
By how much does replacement exceed the upfront outlay limit?
At what annual renewal rent would renewal PV equal the replacement PV, assuming other renewal terms unchanged?
Why does stabilized rent 5m not guarantee the better choice?
qas.answer: Vacancy, fit-out, commission and timing reduce replacement PV; the upfront cap also excludes it.

qas.question: Can fixed overhead .8m be saved by choosing renewal over replacement?
qas.answer: No. It is common to both options.

qas.question: Can future asset market value after year three be estimated from these leases alone?
qas.answer: No. Terminal rent, cap rates and market assumptions are missing.

assumptions: USD million. Fictional fund Moss River. Toy cash redemption due now; sell assets in allowed whole lots only. Sale cash proceeds net fees; portfolio loss = carrying minus net proceeds. Minimize loss while retaining cash floor.

evidence.text: [Cash] Unrestricted cash 18m, confirmed redemption 50m, required post-redemption cash minimum 5m.

[Lots] Liquid bond lot A carrying 25m, cash proceeds 24.8m after fees; equity lot B carrying 20m, proceeds 19m; equity lot C carrying 15m, proceeds 13.5m. Each lot indivisible, all immediately saleable.
[Constraint] No borrowing, no other sales; may choose any subset. No income tax or gain distributions. No price changes beyond quoted proceeds.
[NAV] Opening total NAV 150m including cash/lots and illiquid assets; redemption reduces NAV by actual paid 50m, sale loss reduces NAV independently.
[Policy] Choose subset meeting cash floor and lowest total realized loss. Unneeded cash may be held.
[Memo] Manager sells C first because smallest carrying value and reports redemption itself as investment loss.

qas.question: Find minimum sale proceeds needed to meet redemption and remaining cash floor.
Find proceeds of A+C, and whether they meet cash requirement.
Find loss from A+B combined sale.
Find loss from A+C combined sale.
Find final cash under the minimum-loss feasible subset.
Reconcile closing NAV for the chosen subset, without calling redemption a performance loss.
Explain why C+B cannot be selected despite the combined carrying value 35m.
qas.answer: Net proceeds 32.5m fall below required 37m. Carrying amount is not usable cash proceeds.

qas.question: Can actual investor NAV per unit after redemption be found?
qas.answer: No. Unit counts and redemption price basis are not supplied.
